title: Prefix Echoes
statement: You are given a lowercase string text and a list of lengths. For each length L in lengths, report how many times the prefix text[0..L) occurs inside text as a contiguous substring. Occurrences may overlap, and the prefix itself at position 0 counts as one occurrence. Return the counts in the same order as the lengths.
constraints: 1 <= text.length <= 40000, and text uses only the letters a to z

examples.explanation: The prefix "c" occurs at positions 0, 3, 7 and 10, and "cab" at the same four positions. "cabcab" occurs at positions 0 and 7. "cabcabd" and the whole text each occur once.
"a" occurs 5 times, "aa" starts at positions 0 to 3 so it occurs 4 times, and the whole text occurs once.

hints.content: Imagine the prefix of length L sliding along the text. When it matches somewhere, what does that tell you about the shorter prefixes at that spot?
Comparing the prefix at every start for every query costs O(n * L) per query, and a text like "aaaa..." makes that hopeless. You need to reuse earlier comparisons.
Compute the border array: border[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of text[0..i] that is also a suffix of it.

A prefix of length L occurs ending at position e exactly when L is on the chain e + 1, then border[e], then the border of that prefix, and so on. So each end position adds one occurrence to every length on its chain.

Start with echoes[len] = 1 for every len, then for len from n down to 1 add echoes[len] into echoes[border[len - 1]] when that border is positive. Longer lengths push first, so each total is complete before it is pushed further. Answer each query by lookup: O(n + queries).

testCases.explanation: A text that repeats a block with a different letter in the middle.
No letter repeats, so every prefix occurs once.
A period-2 text: odd and even prefix lengths behave differently.
A block that repeats with a letter in the middle.
A random two-letter text of 200 letters with random query lengths.
The largest input of one repeated letter, where each query checks tens of thousands of overlapping positions.
A 40,000-letter Fibonacci word, which has a very long chain of nested borders.
A 40,000-letter period-2 text with 3,000 random query lengths.

solutions.title: Match the prefix at every start
solutions.intuition: For each query, slide the prefix along the text and compare letter by letter.
solutions.approach: For a query length L, try every start from 0 to n - L and compare up to L letters, counting the starts where all L match.
solutions.pseudocode:
for L in lengths: count = 0
  for start in 0..n-L: if text[start..start+L) == text[0..L): count += 1
solutions.timeComplexity: O(queries * n * L) in the worst case, about 3000 * 40000 * 20000 for one repeated letter
commonMistakes: Starting at 1 and forgetting that the prefix occurs at position 0.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Naive matching is the definition of the task and works for short or random texts, because mismatches appear quickly. A text of one repeated letter forces a full comparison at every start, so each query costs about n * L. The border array lets one linear pass answer every length at once.

steps.title: Query 3
steps.content: For "cab" in "cabcabdcabcab", the comparisons succeed at starts 0, 3, 7 and 10.

steps.title: Other starts
steps.content: All other starts fail within three letters, so the count is 4.

solutions.title: Z-function and a suffix count
solutions.intuition: z[i] is how many letters of the prefix match starting at position i, so the prefix of length L occurs at i exactly when z[i] >= L.
solutions.approach: Compute the Z-array with the standard window algorithm (z[0] = n). Count how many positions have each z value, then turn those counts into suffix sums: atLeast[L] is the number of positions with z >= L. Answer each query with atLeast[L].
solutions.pseudocode:
z = Z-array of text, z[0] = n
count[z[i]] += 1 for each i
for L from n-1 down to 1: count[L] += count[L+1]
answer(L) = count[L]
commonMistakes: Forgetting position 0 (z[0] = n), which is an occurrence of every prefix.
Letting the Z window reuse z[i - left] without capping it at right - i.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The Z-array is the dual of the border array: z[i] directly measures the match with the prefix at position i. An occurrence of the length-L prefix at i is the same as z[i] >= L, so a counting array and a running sum answer every length. Both algorithms are linear; the border version needs the failure-link idea, the Z version needs the matching-window idea.

steps.title: Suffix counts
steps.content: Positions with z >= 1, 2 and 5 are 5, 4 and 1, which are the answers for lengths 1, 2 and 5.

solutions.title: Border array and counts pushed along the chain
solutions.intuition: Every end position of an occurrence of a prefix lies on a chain of borders; counting each end once and pushing the count down the chain gives every prefix's total.
solutions.approach: Compute border[i] with the standard failure-function loop. Set echoes[len] = 1 for every len from 1 to n (the prefix ending at len - 1 is itself an occurrence of that length). For len from n down to 1, add echoes[len] to echoes[border[len - 1]] when that border is positive. Return echoes[L] for each query.
solutions.pseudocode:
border[0] = 0; for i = 1..n-1: k = border[i-1]; while k > 0 and text[i] != text[k]: k = border[k-1]; if text[i] == text[k]: k += 1; border[i] = k
echoes[1..n] = 1
for len = n down to 1: b = border[len-1]; if b > 0: echoes[b] += echoes[len]
answer(L) = echoes[L]
commonMistakes: Pushing from short lengths to long ones, so a total is pushed before it is complete.
Initializing echoes to 0, which forgets that every prefix ending at its own length counts.
Resetting k to 0 on a mismatch instead of following border[k - 1].
solutions.interviewExplanation: An occurrence of the length-L prefix that ends at position e means text[0..L) is a suffix of text[0..e], i.e. L is a border of the prefix of length e + 1. Borders form a chain through the border array, so each prefix length contributes 1 to itself and passes its total to its longest border. Processing lengths from longest to shortest guarantees the total is final when it is pushed. The failure loop is amortized linear.

steps.title: Push counts
steps.content: From echoes [1, 1, 1, 1, 1], length 5 pushes into 4, giving 2; length 4 pushes 2 into 3, giving 3; and so on to 5 at length 1. The answers for 1, 2 and 5 are 5, 4 and 1.
